document.abstract: As SMPTE celebrates turning a spectacular one hundred and ten years old, I have been considering how the future was viewed when we were founded. Motion pictures were, of course, on the rise globally and needed a standard to allow interoperability for film; hence SMPTE was formed. The first photographic film images were made in the late 1830s; a few years later, the stereo photograph was invented. They were viewable using the stereoscope–a single-user device, which gained much popularity in the late 1800s. With the invention of celluloid film, motion pictures emerged about 40 years later, and by the 1910s, the motion picture industry had adopted stereoscopic exhibition for the first time. 3D cinema had many resurgences over the following decades, but its popularity ebbed and flowed, not least because of the complexity of shooting it. With the advent of Digital Cinema, and its ability to be converted to stereoscopic replay, a new burst of 3D activity followed. As consumer formats could also support it, 3D made its way into the home with 3D TVs and some limited stereoscopic broadcasts. However, interest waned, and 3D TVs' moment in the spotlight gave way to UHD, HDR, and streaming. Step forward VR/AR, and 3D is back again. And so it goes almost full circle–almost 200 years after the first stereo photograph was available through a single-viewer device, we find ourselves with stereoscopic motion pictures on single-viewer VR devices. Now, this isn't to say anything about 3D as a format; of course, for most of us, that's how we experience the world visually, and it makes sense to have this as an immersive format for entertainment. And now we can go further. With 3D and 4D scanning, immersive media can transition to free-viewpoint VR. So will this be the moment for stereoscopic 3D to take its place as a permanent fixture of entertainment?
